newsitem.title: FRANCE: France votes sluggishly in snap Assembly poll.
newsitem.headline: France votes sluggishly in snap Assembly poll.

text.p: France voted sluggishly on Sunday in the first round of a parliamentary election that will either renew backing for conservative President Jacques Chirac or condemn him to share power with left-wingers until 2002.
Voter turnout slackened after a relatively brisk start, reviving fears of high abstentions after a lacklustre campaign for the National Assembly.

Turnout at 5 p.m. (1500 GMT) was 54.51 percent of the 39-million-strong electorate. This fell below the 54.7 percent at the same point in 1988 when final turnout was 66.1 percent, the lowest at any National Assembly election since the start of the Fifth Republic in 1958.
Most of the country basked in warm sunshine.

Polling stations close at 8 p.m. (1800 GMT) when first results, and pollsters' predictions of the overall winners next week, will be broadcast. A runoff will take place on June 1 in districts where no candidate has won more than 50 percent support.

Voters had a choice between the ruling centre-right, which promises reforms to scale down state control and a Socialist-led opposition pledging vigorous state job creation and a shorter working week to attack record 12.8 percent joblessness.

Opinion polls published before a legal blackout last week showed that Prime Minister Alain Juppe's coalition was likely to retain power for the next five years, saving Chirac from awkward "cohabitation" with a left-wing government.
But the left was within reach of an upset. A total 6,389 candidates, including a record 1,469 women, vied on Sunday for seats in the 577-seat chamber.

Juppe, shown by opinion polls last year to be the least popular prime minister since 1958, had to submit to an unexpected identity check when he voted in the southwestern city of Bordeaux where he is a candidate.
When a polling official asked him to identify himself, Juppe replied: "Usually, it's enough to be well known". The official refused to budge, obliging Juppe to show his identity card.
Chirac, who called the vote saying France needed a "new elan" to help prepare for a single European currency, voted in Sarran, a village in central France.

Socialist opposition leader Lionel Jospin, who campaigned with the slogan "Let's change the future", voted in Cintegabelle in the southwest where he is hoping to win re-entry to the National Assembly after losing his seat in 1993.

In the capital on Sunday morning, there was a mere trickle of voters into polling stations while markets were crammed with shoppers bent on stocking up with champagne, smoked salmon and chicken for Mothers Day dinners.

Chirac, who gambled in calling the vote 10 months early and two years into his own seven-year term, has said he will not resign if the left wins. But he has warned voters that a period of enforced "cohabitation" could weaken France's voice abroad.

In the troubled Mediterranean island of Corsica, suspected separatists battling for more autonomy from mainland France detonated two bombs that damaged public buildings in Ajaccio and Bastia. No one was hurt.
Juppe has cautioned that the initial results may be hard to interpret -- the combined left could win more of the first-round vote than the centre-right but still end up losing on June 1.

Low turnout might help Juppe by cutting the number of three-way runoffs involving the far-right National Front of Jean-Marie Le Pen, whose voters tend to opt for the centre-right if their candidate is eliminated.

Candidates need the support of 12.5 percent of all registered voters to reach the second-round runoffs. If turnout matches that of 1988, a candidate would need 19 percent of the votes cast to reach the second round.
On the other hand, low turnout might also signal that voters are turning to protest parties like the anti-immigrant Front.

Juppe said he would maintain his austerity policies to help France qualify for a single European currency. He promised a public spending freeze, tax cuts, an accelerated privatisation programme and a reduction in both the size and role of the civil service to give more scope for private initiative.

The Socialist and Communist opposition said it would cut unemployment, the highest among the Group of Seven industrial nations, by creating 700,000 youth jobs and reducing the work week from 39 to 35 hours without loss of pay.
Jospin has ruled out taking any further austerity measures to enable France to qualify for the euro common currency from its creation in 1999.
